&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The accompanying unaudited consolidated financial statements of Schlumberger Limited and its subsidiaries (&#x201c;Schlumberger&#x201d;) have been prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America for interim financial information and with the instructions to Form 10-Q and Article 10 of Regulation S-X.&#160;&#160;Accordingly, they do not include all of the information and footnotes required by generally accepted accounting principles for complete financial statements.&#160;&#160;In the opinion of Schlumberger management, all adjustments considered necessary for a fair statement have been included in the accompanying unaudited financial statements.&#160;&#160;All intercompany transactions and balances have been eliminated in consolidation.&#160;&#160;Operating results for the nine-month period ended September 30, 2020 are not necessarily indicative of the results that may be expected for the full year ending December&#160;31, 2020.&#160;&#160;The December&#160;31, 2019 balance sheet information has been derived from the Schlumberger 2019 audited financial statements.&#160;&#160;For further information, refer to the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Financial Statements&lt;/span&gt; and notes thereto included in the Schlumberger Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December&#160;31, 2019, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on January&#160;22, 2020. &lt;/p&gt;

(&#x201c;Liberty&#x201d;) entered into an agreement for the contribution to Liberty of OneStim&lt;sup style="font-size:85%;line-height:120%;vertical-align:top"&gt;&#xae;&lt;/sup&gt;,&lt;sup style="font-size:85%;line-height:120%;vertical-align:top"&gt; &lt;/sup&gt;Schlumberger&#x2019;s onshore hydraulic fracturing business in the United States and Canada, including its pressure pumping, pumpdown perforating, and Permian frac sand businesses, in exchange for a 37% equity interest in Liberty.&#160;&#160;The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2020 and is subject to Liberty stockholder approval and other customary closing conditions.&#160;&#160;OneStim represented approximately 5% of Schlumberger&#x2019;s consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2020.&lt;/p&gt;</us-gaap:OrganizationConsolidationAndPresentationOfFinancialStatementsDisclosureTextBlock>

&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:12pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;First quarter 2020:&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:6pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div style="align:left;"&gt;
&lt;table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;"&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&#x2022;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;Geopolitical events that increased the supply of low-priced oil to the global market occurred at the same time that demand weakened due to the worldwide effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to a collapse in oil prices during March 2020.&#160;&#160;As a result, Schlumberger&#x2019;s market capitalization deteriorated significantly compared to the end of 2019.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#x2019;s stock price reached a low during the first quarter of 2020 not seen since 1995.&#160;&#160;Additionally, the Philadelphia Oil Services Sector index, which is comprised of companies involved in the oil services sector, reached an all-time low.&#160;&#160;As a result of these facts, Schlumberger determined that it was more likely than not that the fair value of certain of its reporting units were less than their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Therefore, Schlumberger performed an interim goodwill impairment test.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;&lt;/tr&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger had 11 reporting units with goodwill balances aggregating $16.0 billion.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger determined that the fair value of four of its reporting units, representing $4.5 billion of the goodwill, was substantially in excess of their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger performed a detailed quantitative impairment assessment of the remaining seven reporting units, which represented $11.5 billion of goodwill. As a result of this assessment, Schlumberger concluded that the goodwill associated with each of these seven reporting units was impaired, resulting in a $3.1 billion goodwill impairment charge.&#160;&#160;This charge primarily relates to goodwill associated with the Drilling and Production segments.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Following the $3.1 billion goodwill impairment charge relating to these seven reporting units, six of these reporting units had a remaining goodwill balance.&#160;&#160;These six reporting units had goodwill balances which ranged between $0.2 billion and $5.0 billion and aggregated to $8.4 billion as of March 31, 2020. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger used the income approach to estimate the fair value of its reporting units, but also considered the market approach to validate the results.&#160;&#160;The income approach estimates the fair value by discounting each reporting unit&#x2019;s estimated future cash flows using Schlumberger&#x2019;s estimate of the discount rate, or expected return, that a marketplace participant would have required as of the valuation date.&#160;&#160;The market approach includes the use of comparative multiples to corroborate the discounted cash flow results. The market approach involves significant judgement involved in the selection of the appropriate peer group companies and valuation multiples.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Some of the more significant assumptions inherent in the income approach include the estimated future net annual cash flows for each reporting unit and the discount rate.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger selected the assumptions used in the discounted cash flow projections using historical data supplemented by current and anticipated market conditions and estimated growth rates.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#x2019;s estimates are based upon assumptions believed to be reasonable.&#160;&#160;However, given the inherent uncertainty in determining the assumptions underlying a discounted cash flow analysis, particularly in the current volatile market, actual results may differ from those used in Schlumberger&#x2019;s valuations which could result in additional impairment charges in the future.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The discount rates utilized to value Schlumberger&#x2019;s reporting units were between 12.0% and 13.5%, depending on the risks and uncertainty inherent in the respective reporting unit as well as the size of the reporting unit.&#160;&#160;Assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50-basis point increase or decrease in the discount rate assumptions would have changed the fair value of the seven reporting units, on average, by less than 5%.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div style="align:left;"&gt;
&lt;table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;"&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;td valign="top"&gt;

&lt;p style="text-align:right;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:0pt;;text-indent:0pt;;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;11,979&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="background-color:#CFF0FC;padding-left:0pt;padding-Right:0.75pt;padding-Top:0.75pt;width:0.98%; border-bottom:double 2.5pt transparent;white-space:nowrap;" valign="bottom"&gt;
&lt;p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:0pt;;text-indent:0pt;;color:#000000;font-size:1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;"&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&#x2022;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;During August 2019, Schlumberger&#x2019;s market capitalization deteriorated significantly compared to the end of the second quarter of 2019.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#x2019;s stock price reached a low not seen since 2005.&#160;&#160;Additionally, the Philadelphia Oil Services Sector Index, which is comprised of companies involved in the oil services sector, reached an 18-year low.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;&lt;/tr&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;As a result of these facts, Schlumberger determined that it was more likely than not that the fair value of certain of its reporting units were less than their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Therefore, Schlumberger performed an interim goodwill impairment test as of August 31, 2019.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;As of August 31, 2019, Schlumberger had 17 reporting units with goodwill balances aggregating $25.0 billion.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger determined that the fair value of seven of its reporting units, representing approximately $13.8 billion of the goodwill, was substantially in excess of their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger performed a detailed quantitative impairment assessment of the remaining 10 reporting units, which represented $11.2 billion of goodwill. As a result of this assessment, Schlumberger concluded that the goodwill associated with nine of the 10 reporting units was impaired, resulting in an $8.8 billion goodwill impairment charge.&#160;&#160;This charge primarily relates to Schlumberger&#x2019;s Drilling and Cameron segments.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Following the $8.8 billion goodwill impairment charge relating to these nine reporting units, only three had a remaining goodwill balance.&#160;&#160;These three reporting units had goodwill balances which ranged between $0.4 billion and $0.6 billion and aggregated to $1.5 billion as of August 31, 2019. The tenth reporting unit, which was determined not to be impaired, had $0.9 billion of goodwill.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger primarily used the income approach to estimate the fair value of its reporting units, but also considered the market approach to validate the results.&#160;&#160;The income approach estimates the fair value by discounting each reporting unit&#x2019;s estimated future cash flows using Schlumberger&#x2019;s estimate of the discount rate, or expected return, that a marketplace participant would have required as of the valuation date.&#160;&#160;The market approach includes the use of comparative multiples to corroborate the discounted cash flow results.&#160;&#160;The market approach involves significant judgement involved in the selection of the appropriate peer group companies and valuation multiples.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Some of the more significant assumptions inherent in the income approach include the estimated future net annual cash flows for each reporting unit and the discount rate.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger selected the assumptions used in the discounted cash flow projections using historical data supplemented by current and anticipated market conditions and estimated growth rates.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#x2019;s estimates are based upon assumptions believed to be reasonable.&#160;&#160;However, given the inherent uncertainty in determining the assumptions underlying a discounted cash flow analysis, actual results may differ from those used in Schlumberger&#x2019;s valuations which could result in additional impairment charges in the future.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The discount rates utilized to value Schlumberger&#x2019;s reporting units were between 12.5% and 14.0%, depending on the risks and uncertainty inherent in the respective reporting unit.&#160;&#160;Assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50 basis point increase in the discount rate assumption would have increased the goodwill impairment charge by approximately $0.3 billion.&#160;&#160;Conversely, assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50 basis point decrease in the discount rate assumption would have decreased the goodwill impairment charge by approximately $0.4 billion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:10pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&#x2022;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td valign="top"&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:10pt;margin-bottom:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"/&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"/&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;The negative market indicators described above&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt; combined with deteriorating market conditions in North America, as well as the results of the previously mentioned fair value determinations of certain of Schlumberger&#x2019;s reporting units and the appointment of a new Chief Executive Officer (as described below), were all triggering events that indicated that certain of Schlumberger&#x2019;s long-lived tangible and intangible assets may &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;have &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;be&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt;en&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="font-family:Times New Roman;"&gt; impaired.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/td&gt;&lt;/tr&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Recoverability testing, which was performed as of August 31, 2019, indicated that long-lived assets associated with certain asset groups were impaired.&#160;&#160;The estimated fair value of these asset groups was determined to be below their carrying value.&#160;&#160;As a result, Schlumberger recorded the following impairment and related charges:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The estimated fair value of Schlumberger&#x2019;s &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Long-term Debt, &lt;/span&gt;based on quoted market prices at September 30, 2020 and December 31, 2019, was $17.2 billion and $15.3 billion, respectively.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger entered into a &#x20ac;1.54 billion committed revolving credit facility.&#160;&#160;This &lt;span style="-sec-ix-hidden:F_000899"&gt;one-year&lt;/span&gt; facility can be extended at Schlumberger&#x2019;s option for up to an additional year.&#160;&#160;&lt;span style="color:#000000;"&gt;At September 30, 2020 &lt;/span&gt;no amounts had been drawn under this facility.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had separate committed credit facility agreements aggregating $8.06 billion with commercial banks, of which $6.98 billion was available and unused. &#160;These committed facilities support commercial paper programs in the United States and Europe, of which $1.81 billion matures in April 2021, $2.75 billion matures in February 2023, $2.0 billion matures in February 2025 and $1.5 billion matures in July 2025 &lt;span style="color:#000000;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/span&gt;.&#160;&#160;Interest rates and other terms of borrowing under these lines of credit vary by facility.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Borrowings under the commercial paper programs at September 30, 2020 were $1.08 billion, all of which&#160;was classified in&#160;&lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Long-term debt&lt;/span&gt; in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span style="color:#000000;"&gt;Sheet&lt;/span&gt;.&#160;&#160;At December 31, 2019, borrowings under the commercial paper programs were $2.22 billion, all of which was classified in &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Long-term debt&lt;/span&gt; in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet&lt;/span&gt;.  &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the first quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;400 million of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#x20ac;400 million of 0.50% Notes due 2031.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;1.0 billion of 1.375% Guaranteed Notes due 2026, $900 million of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2030 and &#x20ac;1.0 billion of 2.00% Guaranteed Notes due 2032.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger repurchased all $600 million of its 4.20% Senior Notes due 2021 and $935 million of its 3.30% Senior Notes due 2021.&#160; Schlumberger paid a premium of approximately $40 million in connection with these repurchases.&#160; This premium was classified in &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Impairments &amp;amp; other&lt;/span&gt; in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Loss&lt;/span&gt;.&#160; See Note 2 &#x2013; &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Charges and Credits&lt;/span&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger established a &#x20ac;5.0 billion Guaranteed Euro Medium Term Note program that provides for the issuance of various types of debt instruments such as fixed or floating rate notes in euro, US dollar or other currencies.&#160; At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had not issued any debt under this program.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the third quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued $500 million of 1.40% Senior Notes due 2025 and $350 million of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2030.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:2pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the third quarter of 2019, Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;500 million of 0.00% Notes due 2024, &#x20ac;500 million of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#x20ac;500 million of 0.50% Notes due 2031.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;In September 2019, Schlumberger repurchased $783 million of its 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020 and $321 million of its 3.625% Senior Notes due 2022. Schlumberger paid a premium of $29 million in connection with these repurchases. This premium was classified as &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Impairments &amp;amp; other&lt;/span&gt; in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Loss&lt;/span&gt;. (See Note 2 - &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Charges and Credits.&lt;/span&gt;)&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;In April 2019, Schlumberger completed a debt exchange offer, pursuant to which it issued $1.500 billion in principal of 3.90% Senior Notes due 2028 (the &#x201c;New Notes&#x201d;) in exchange for $401 million of 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020, $234 million of 3.63% Senior Notes due 2022 and $817 million of 4.00% Senior Notes due 2025.&#160; In connection with the exchange of principal, Schlumberger paid a premium of $48 million, substantially all of which was in the form of New Notes.&#160; This premium is being amortized as additional interest expense over the term of the New Notes&lt;span style="color:#000000;"&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt;

    <us-gaap:DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureTextBlock contextRef="C_0000087347_20200101_20200930" id="F_000452">
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;10.&#160;&#160; &lt;span style="text-decoration:underline;"&gt;Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities&lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to market risks related to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.&#160; To mitigate these risks, Schlumberger utilizes derivative instruments.&#160; Schlumberger does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Interest Rate Risk &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is subject to interest rate risk on its debt and its investment portfolio.&#160; Schlumberger maintains an interest rate risk management strategy that uses a mix of variable and fixed rate debt combined with its investment portfolio, to mitigate the exposure to changes in interest rates.&#160; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had fixed rate debt aggregating $16.6 billion and variable rate debt aggregating $1.2 billion. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Foreign Currency Exchange Rate Risk &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;As a multinational company, Schlumberger generates revenue in more than 120 countries. Schlumberger&#x2019;s functional currency is primarily the US dollar.&#160; However, outside the United States, a significant portion of Schlumberger&#x2019;s expenses are incurred in foreign currencies.&#160; Therefore, when the US dollar weakens (strengthens) in relation to the foreign currencies of the countries in which Schlumberger conducts business, the US dollar-reported expenses will increase (decrease).&#160;&#160; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to risks on future cash flows to the extent that the local currency is not the functional currency and expenses denominated in local currency are not equal to revenues denominated in local currency.&#160; Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts to provide a hedge against a portion of these cash flow risks.&#160; These contracts are accounted for as cash flow hedges, with the changes in the fair value of the hedge recorded on the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet &lt;/span&gt;and in &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss.&#160; &lt;/span&gt;Amounts recorded in&lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt; Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss &lt;/span&gt;are reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods that the hedged item is recognized in earnings.&#160; &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is also exposed to risks on future cash flows relating to certain of its fixed rate debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. Schlumberger uses cross-currency swaps to provide a hedge against these cash flow risks. &lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During 2017, a Canadian-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $1.1 billion of US-dollar denominated debt.&#160; Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $1.1 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion of 2.20% Senior Notes due 2020 and its $0.6 billion of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2022.&#160;&#160;These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US-dollar denominated notes to Canadian-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.97% and 2.52%, respectively.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During 2019, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;1.5 billion of Euro-denominated debt.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#x20ac;1.5 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#x20ac;0.5 billion 0.00% Notes due 2024, &#x20ac;0.5 billion 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#x20ac;0.5 billion 0.50% Notes due 2031. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 2.29%, 2.51% and 2.76%, respectively.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the first quarter of 2020, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;0.8 billion of Euro-denominated debt. Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#x20ac;0.8 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#x20ac;0.4 billion of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#x20ac;0.4 billion of 0.50% Notes due 2031. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.87% and 2.20%, respectively. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the second quarter of 2020, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#x20ac;2.0 billion of Euro-denominated debt. Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#x20ac;1.85 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#x20ac;1.0 billion of 1.375% Guaranteed Notes due 2026 and &#x20ac;0.85 billion of 2.00% Guaranteed Notes due 2032. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the swapped portion of the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 2.77% and 3.45%, respectively. Schlumberger hedged its exposure to currency fluctuations on the remaining &#x20ac;0.15 billion of Euro-denominated debt issued by using foreign currency forward contracts that are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;During the third quarter of 2020, a Canadian dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $0.5 billion of US dollar denominated debt.&#160; Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $0.5 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion 1.40% Senior Notes due 2025. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US dollar notes to Canadian dollar denominated debt with a fixed annual interest rate of 1.73%.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Schlumberger is exposed to changes in the fair value of assets and liabilities that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&#160; While Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts and foreign currency options to economically hedge this exposure as it relates to certain currencies, these contracts are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.&#160; Instead, the fair value of the contracts is recorded on the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Balance Sheet, &lt;/span&gt;and changes in the fair value are recognized in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Loss &lt;/span&gt;as are changes in fair value of the hedged item.&#160;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At September 30, 2020, contracts were outstanding for the US dollar equivalent of $10.9 billion in various foreign currencies, of which $6.7 billion relates to hedges of debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger recognized a cumulative $218 million loss in &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss&lt;/span&gt; relating to changes in the fair value of foreign currency forward contracts and cross-currency swaps.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;The effect of derivative instruments designated as cash flow hedges, and those not designated as hedges, on the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Loss &lt;/span&gt;was as follows: &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:12pt;"&gt;&#160;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"&gt;Due to the actions taken by Schlumberger to reduce its global workforce during 2020, Schlumberger experienced a significant reduction in the expected aggregate years of future service of its employees in its US postretirement medical plan. Accordingly, Schlumberger recorded a curtailment gain of $69 million during the second quarter of 2020 relating to this plan. The curtailment gain includes recognition of the decrease in the benefit obligation as well as a portion of the previously unrecognized prior service credit, reflecting the reduction in expected years of future service.&#160; As a result of the curtailment, Schlumberger performed a remeasurement of the plan, which had an immaterial impact.&#160; This gain was classified in &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Impairments &amp;amp; other&lt;/span&gt; in the &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Consolidated Statement of Loss&lt;/span&gt;.&#160; See Note 2 &#x2013; &lt;span style="font-style:italic;"&gt;Charges and Credits&lt;/span&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

<tr><td class="hide"><a style="color: white;" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.hideAR();">X</a></td></tr>
<tr><td><div class="body" style="padding: 2px;">
<a href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.toggleNext( this );">- Definition</a><div><p>Total of all stockholders' equity (deficit) items, net of receivables from officers, directors, owners, and affiliates of the entity which are attributable to the parent. The amount of the economic entity's stockholders' equity attributable to the parent excludes the amount of stockholders' equity which is allocable to that ownership interest in subsidiary equity which is not attributable to the parent (noncontrolling interest, minority interest). This excludes temporary equity and is sometimes called permanent equity.</p></div>

<td class="text">
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">1.&#160;&#160; <span style="text-decoration:underline;">Basis of Presentation</span> </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The accompanying unaudited consolidated financial statements of Schlumberger Limited and its subsidiaries (&#8220;Schlumberger&#8221;) have been prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America for interim financial information and with the instructions to Form 10-Q and Article 10 of Regulation S-X.&#160;&#160;Accordingly, they do not include all of the information and footnotes required by generally accepted accounting principles for complete financial statements.&#160;&#160;In the opinion of Schlumberger management, all adjustments considered necessary for a fair statement have been included in the accompanying unaudited financial statements.&#160;&#160;All intercompany transactions and balances have been eliminated in consolidation.&#160;&#160;Operating results for the nine-month period ended September 30, 2020 are not necessarily indicative of the results that may be expected for the full year ending December&#160;31, 2020.&#160;&#160;The December&#160;31, 2019 balance sheet information has been derived from the Schlumberger 2019 audited financial statements.&#160;&#160;For further information, refer to the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Financial Statements</span> and notes thereto included in the Schlumberger Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December&#160;31, 2019, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on January&#160;22, 2020. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">On August 31, 2020, Schlumberger and Liberty Oilfield Services Inc. (&#8220;Liberty&#8221;) entered into an agreement for the contribution to Liberty of OneStim<sup style="font-size:85%;line-height:120%;vertical-align:top">&#174;</sup>,<sup style="font-size:85%;line-height:120%;vertical-align:top"> </sup>Schlumberger&#8217;s onshore hydraulic fracturing business in the United States and Canada, including its pressure pumping, pumpdown perforating, and Permian frac sand businesses, in exchange for a 37% equity interest in Liberty.&#160;&#160;The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2020 and is subject to Liberty stockholder approval and other customary closing conditions.&#160;&#160;OneStim represented approximately 5% of Schlumberger&#8217;s consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2020.</p><span></span>

<p style="text-align:right;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:0pt;;text-indent:0pt;;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">11,539</p></td>
<td style="background-color:#FFFFFF;padding-left:0pt;padding-Right:0.75pt;padding-Top:0.75pt;width:1%; border-bottom:double 2.5pt transparent;white-space:nowrap;" valign="bottom">
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:0pt;;text-indent:0pt;;color:#000000;font-size:1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p></td>

<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:12pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:6pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><span style="font-style:italic;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">First quarter 2020:</span></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:6pt;">&#160;</p>
<div style="align:left;">
<table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;">
<tr>
<td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p></td>
<td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#8226;</span></p></td>
<td valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"><span style="font-family:Times New Roman;">Geopolitical events that increased the supply of low-priced oil to the global market occurred at the same time that demand weakened due to the worldwide effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to a collapse in oil prices during March 2020.&#160;&#160;As a result, Schlumberger&#8217;s market capitalization deteriorated significantly compared to the end of 2019.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#8217;s stock price reached a low during the first quarter of 2020 not seen since 1995.&#160;&#160;Additionally, the Philadelphia Oil Services Sector index, which is comprised of companies involved in the oil services sector, reached an all-time low.&#160;&#160;As a result of these facts, Schlumberger determined that it was more likely than not that the fair value of certain of its reporting units were less than their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Therefore, Schlumberger performed an interim goodwill impairment test.</span></p></td></tr></table></div>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger had 11 reporting units with goodwill balances aggregating $16.0 billion.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger determined that the fair value of four of its reporting units, representing $4.5 billion of the goodwill, was substantially in excess of their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger performed a detailed quantitative impairment assessment of the remaining seven reporting units, which represented $11.5 billion of goodwill. As a result of this assessment, Schlumberger concluded that the goodwill associated with each of these seven reporting units was impaired, resulting in a $3.1 billion goodwill impairment charge.&#160;&#160;This charge primarily relates to goodwill associated with the Drilling and Production segments.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Following the $3.1 billion goodwill impairment charge relating to these seven reporting units, six of these reporting units had a remaining goodwill balance.&#160;&#160;These six reporting units had goodwill balances which ranged between $0.2 billion and $5.0 billion and aggregated to $8.4 billion as of March 31, 2020. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger used the income approach to estimate the fair value of its reporting units, but also considered the market approach to validate the results.&#160;&#160;The income approach estimates the fair value by discounting each reporting unit&#8217;s estimated future cash flows using Schlumberger&#8217;s estimate of the discount rate, or expected return, that a marketplace participant would have required as of the valuation date.&#160;&#160;The market approach includes the use of comparative multiples to corroborate the discounted cash flow results. The market approach involves significant judgement involved in the selection of the appropriate peer group companies and valuation multiples.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Some of the more significant assumptions inherent in the income approach include the estimated future net annual cash flows for each reporting unit and the discount rate.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger selected the assumptions used in the discounted cash flow projections using historical data supplemented by current and anticipated market conditions and estimated growth rates.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#8217;s estimates are based upon assumptions believed to be reasonable.&#160;&#160;However, given the inherent uncertainty in determining the assumptions underlying a discounted cash flow analysis, particularly in the current volatile market, actual results may differ from those used in Schlumberger&#8217;s valuations which could result in additional impairment charges in the future.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The discount rates utilized to value Schlumberger&#8217;s reporting units were between 12.0% and 13.5%, depending on the risks and uncertainty inherent in the respective reporting unit as well as the size of the reporting unit.&#160;&#160;Assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50-basis point increase or decrease in the discount rate assumptions would have changed the fair value of the seven reporting units, on average, by less than 5%.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>

<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-left:0pt;;text-indent:0pt;;color:#000000;font-size:1pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p></td>

<div style="align:left;">
<table border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:100%;">
<tr>
<td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p></td>
<td style="width:3.33%;white-space:nowrap" valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><span style="font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#8226;</span></p></td>
<td valign="top">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;font-family:'Times New Roman';font-size:10pt;"><span style="font-family:Times New Roman;">During August 2019, Schlumberger&#8217;s market capitalization deteriorated significantly compared to the end of the second quarter of 2019.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#8217;s stock price reached a low not seen since 2005.&#160;&#160;Additionally, the Philadelphia Oil Services Sector Index, which is comprised of companies involved in the oil services sector, reached an 18-year low.</span></p></td></tr></table></div>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As a result of these facts, Schlumberger determined that it was more likely than not that the fair value of certain of its reporting units were less than their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Therefore, Schlumberger performed an interim goodwill impairment test as of August 31, 2019.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As of August 31, 2019, Schlumberger had 17 reporting units with goodwill balances aggregating $25.0 billion.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger determined that the fair value of seven of its reporting units, representing approximately $13.8 billion of the goodwill, was substantially in excess of their carrying value.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger performed a detailed quantitative impairment assessment of the remaining 10 reporting units, which represented $11.2 billion of goodwill. As a result of this assessment, Schlumberger concluded that the goodwill associated with nine of the 10 reporting units was impaired, resulting in an $8.8 billion goodwill impairment charge.&#160;&#160;This charge primarily relates to Schlumberger&#8217;s Drilling and Cameron segments.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Following the $8.8 billion goodwill impairment charge relating to these nine reporting units, only three had a remaining goodwill balance.&#160;&#160;These three reporting units had goodwill balances which ranged between $0.4 billion and $0.6 billion and aggregated to $1.5 billion as of August 31, 2019. The tenth reporting unit, which was determined not to be impaired, had $0.9 billion of goodwill.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger primarily used the income approach to estimate the fair value of its reporting units, but also considered the market approach to validate the results.&#160;&#160;The income approach estimates the fair value by discounting each reporting unit&#8217;s estimated future cash flows using Schlumberger&#8217;s estimate of the discount rate, or expected return, that a marketplace participant would have required as of the valuation date.&#160;&#160;The market approach includes the use of comparative multiples to corroborate the discounted cash flow results.&#160;&#160;The market approach involves significant judgement involved in the selection of the appropriate peer group companies and valuation multiples.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Some of the more significant assumptions inherent in the income approach include the estimated future net annual cash flows for each reporting unit and the discount rate.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger selected the assumptions used in the discounted cash flow projections using historical data supplemented by current and anticipated market conditions and estimated growth rates.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger&#8217;s estimates are based upon assumptions believed to be reasonable.&#160;&#160;However, given the inherent uncertainty in determining the assumptions underlying a discounted cash flow analysis, actual results may differ from those used in Schlumberger&#8217;s valuations which could result in additional impairment charges in the future.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-left:6.67%;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The discount rates utilized to value Schlumberger&#8217;s reporting units were between 12.5% and 14.0%, depending on the risks and uncertainty inherent in the respective reporting unit.&#160;&#160;Assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50 basis point increase in the discount rate assumption would have increased the goodwill impairment charge by approximately $0.3 billion.&#160;&#160;Conversely, assuming all other assumptions and inputs used in each of the respective discounted cash flow analysis were held constant, a 50 basis point decrease in the discount rate assumption would have decreased the goodwill impairment charge by approximately $0.4 billion.</p>

<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The estimated fair value of Schlumberger&#8217;s <span style="font-style:italic;">Long-term Debt, </span>based on quoted market prices at September 30, 2020 and December 31, 2019, was $17.2 billion and $15.3 billion, respectively.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger entered into a &#8364;1.54 billion committed revolving credit facility.&#160;&#160;This <span style="-sec-ix-hidden:F_000899">one-year</span> facility can be extended at Schlumberger&#8217;s option for up to an additional year.&#160;&#160;<span style="color:#000000;">At September 30, 2020 </span>no amounts had been drawn under this facility.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had separate committed credit facility agreements aggregating $8.06 billion with commercial banks, of which $6.98 billion was available and unused. &#160;These committed facilities support commercial paper programs in the United States and Europe, of which $1.81 billion matures in April 2021, $2.75 billion matures in February 2023, $2.0 billion matures in February 2025 and $1.5 billion matures in July 2025 <span style="color:#000000;">&#160;</span>.&#160;&#160;Interest rates and other terms of borrowing under these lines of credit vary by facility.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Borrowings under the commercial paper programs at September 30, 2020 were $1.08 billion, all of which&#160;was classified in&#160;<span style="font-style:italic;">Long-term debt</span> in the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance </span><span style="color:#000000;">Sheet</span>.&#160;&#160;At December 31, 2019, borrowings under the commercial paper programs were $2.22 billion, all of which was classified in <span style="font-style:italic;">Long-term debt</span> in the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet</span>.  </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the first quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued &#8364;400 million of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#8364;400 million of 0.50% Notes due 2031.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued &#8364;1.0 billion of 1.375% Guaranteed Notes due 2026, $900 million of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2030 and &#8364;1.0 billion of 2.00% Guaranteed Notes due 2032.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger repurchased all $600 million of its 4.20% Senior Notes due 2021 and $935 million of its 3.30% Senior Notes due 2021.&#160; Schlumberger paid a premium of approximately $40 million in connection with these repurchases.&#160; This premium was classified in <span style="font-style:italic;">Impairments &amp; other</span> in the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Loss</span>.&#160; See Note 2 &#8211; <span style="font-style:italic;">Charges and Credits</span>.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the second quarter of 2020, Schlumberger established a &#8364;5.0 billion Guaranteed Euro Medium Term Note program that provides for the issuance of various types of debt instruments such as fixed or floating rate notes in euro, US dollar or other currencies.&#160; At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had not issued any debt under this program.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the third quarter of 2020, Schlumberger issued $500 million of 1.40% Senior Notes due 2025 and $350 million of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2030.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:2pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the third quarter of 2019, Schlumberger issued &#8364;500 million of 0.00% Notes due 2024, &#8364;500 million of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#8364;500 million of 0.50% Notes due 2031.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:2pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In September 2019, Schlumberger repurchased $783 million of its 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020 and $321 million of its 3.625% Senior Notes due 2022. Schlumberger paid a premium of $29 million in connection with these repurchases. This premium was classified as <span style="font-style:italic;">Impairments &amp; other</span> in the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Loss</span>. (See Note 2 - <span style="font-style:italic;">Charges and Credits.</span>)</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">In April 2019, Schlumberger completed a debt exchange offer, pursuant to which it issued $1.500 billion in principal of 3.90% Senior Notes due 2028 (the &#8220;New Notes&#8221;) in exchange for $401 million of 3.00% Senior Notes due 2020, $234 million of 3.63% Senior Notes due 2022 and $817 million of 4.00% Senior Notes due 2025.&#160; In connection with the exchange of principal, Schlumberger paid a premium of $48 million, substantially all of which was in the form of New Notes.&#160; This premium is being amortized as additional interest expense over the term of the New Notes<span style="color:#000000;">.</span> </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:0pt;text-indent:0%;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger Limited fully and unconditionally guarantees the securities issued by certain of its subsidiaries, including securities issued by Schlumberger Investment SA and Schlumberger Finance Canada Ltd., both wholly-owned subsidiaries of Schlumberger.</p><span></span>

<th class="tl" colspan="1" rowspan="2"><div style="width: 200px;"><strong>Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities<br></strong></div></th>
<th class="th" colspan="1">9 Months Ended</th>
</tr>
<tr><th class="th"><div>Sep. 30, 2020</div></th></tr>
<tr class="re">
<td class="pl " style="border-bottom: 0px;" valign="top"><a class="a" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.showAR( this, 'defref_us-gaap_DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureAbstract', window );"><strong>Derivative Instruments And Hedging Activities Disclosure [Abstract]</strong></a></td>
<td class="text">&#160;<span></span>
</td>
</tr>
<tr class="ro">
<td class="pl " style="border-bottom: 0px;" valign="top"><a class="a" href="javascript:void(0);" onclick="top.Show.showAR( this, 'defref_us-gaap_DerivativeInstrumentsAndHedgingActivitiesDisclosureTextBlock', window );">Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities</a></td>
<td class="text">
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">10.&#160;&#160; <span style="text-decoration:underline;">Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities</span> </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to market risks related to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.&#160; To mitigate these risks, Schlumberger utilizes derivative instruments.&#160; Schlumberger does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Interest Rate Risk </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is subject to interest rate risk on its debt and its investment portfolio.&#160; Schlumberger maintains an interest rate risk management strategy that uses a mix of variable and fixed rate debt combined with its investment portfolio, to mitigate the exposure to changes in interest rates.&#160; </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger had fixed rate debt aggregating $16.6 billion and variable rate debt aggregating $1.2 billion. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:18pt;text-indent:0%;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Foreign Currency Exchange Rate Risk </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:6pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">As a multinational company, Schlumberger generates revenue in more than 120 countries. Schlumberger&#8217;s functional currency is primarily the US dollar.&#160; However, outside the United States, a significant portion of Schlumberger&#8217;s expenses are incurred in foreign currencies.&#160; Therefore, when the US dollar weakens (strengthens) in relation to the foreign currencies of the countries in which Schlumberger conducts business, the US dollar-reported expenses will increase (decrease).&#160;&#160; </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to risks on future cash flows to the extent that the local currency is not the functional currency and expenses denominated in local currency are not equal to revenues denominated in local currency.&#160; Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts to provide a hedge against a portion of these cash flow risks.&#160; These contracts are accounted for as cash flow hedges, with the changes in the fair value of the hedge recorded on the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet </span>and in <span style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss.&#160; </span>Amounts recorded in<span style="font-style:italic;"> Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss </span>are reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods that the hedged item is recognized in earnings.&#160; </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;"><span style="font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is also exposed to risks on future cash flows relating to certain of its fixed rate debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. Schlumberger uses cross-currency swaps to provide a hedge against these cash flow risks. </span></p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During 2017, a Canadian-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $1.1 billion of US-dollar denominated debt.&#160; Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $1.1 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion of 2.20% Senior Notes due 2020 and its $0.6 billion of 2.65% Senior Notes due 2022.&#160;&#160;These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US-dollar denominated notes to Canadian-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.97% and 2.52%, respectively.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During 2019, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#8364;1.5 billion of Euro-denominated debt.&#160;&#160;Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#8364;1.5 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#8364;0.5 billion 0.00% Notes due 2024, &#8364;0.5 billion 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#8364;0.5 billion 0.50% Notes due 2031. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 2.29%, 2.51% and 2.76%, respectively.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the first quarter of 2020, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#8364;0.8 billion of Euro-denominated debt. Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#8364;0.8 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#8364;0.4 billion of 0.25% Notes due 2027 and &#8364;0.4 billion of 0.50% Notes due 2031. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 1.87% and 2.20%, respectively. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the second quarter of 2020, a US-dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued &#8364;2.0 billion of Euro-denominated debt. Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of &#8364;1.85 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its &#8364;1.0 billion of 1.375% Guaranteed Notes due 2026 and &#8364;0.85 billion of 2.00% Guaranteed Notes due 2032. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the swapped portion of the Euro-denominated notes to US-dollar denominated debt with fixed annual interest rates of 2.77% and 3.45%, respectively. Schlumberger hedged its exposure to currency fluctuations on the remaining &#8364;0.15 billion of Euro-denominated debt issued by using foreign currency forward contracts that are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">During the third quarter of 2020, a Canadian dollar functional currency subsidiary of Schlumberger issued $0.5 billion of US dollar denominated debt.&#160; Schlumberger entered into cross-currency swaps for an aggregate notional amount of $0.5 billion in order to hedge changes in the fair value of its $0.5 billion 1.40% Senior Notes due 2025. These cross-currency swaps effectively convert the US dollar notes to Canadian dollar denominated debt with a fixed annual interest rate of 1.73%.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">Schlumberger is exposed to changes in the fair value of assets and liabilities that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency.&#160; While Schlumberger uses foreign currency forward contracts and foreign currency options to economically hedge this exposure as it relates to certain currencies, these contracts are not designated as hedges for accounting purposes.&#160; Instead, the fair value of the contracts is recorded on the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Balance Sheet, </span>and changes in the fair value are recognized in the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Loss </span>as are changes in fair value of the hedged item.&#160;&#160;</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At September 30, 2020, contracts were outstanding for the US dollar equivalent of $10.9 billion in various foreign currencies, of which $6.7 billion relates to hedges of debt denominated in currencies other than the functional currency. </p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">At September 30, 2020, Schlumberger recognized a cumulative $218 million loss in <span style="font-style:italic;">Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss</span> relating to changes in the fair value of foreign currency forward contracts and cross-currency swaps.</p>
<p style="text-align:justify;margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:12pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-weight:normal;font-style:normal;text-transform:none;font-variant: normal;">The effect of derivative instruments designated as cash flow hedges, and those not designated as hedges, on the <span style="font-style:italic;">Consolidated Statement of Loss </span>was as follows: </p>
<p style="margin-bottom:0pt;margin-top:0pt;text-indent:0%;font-size:10pt;">&#160;</p>
